question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Found it!

In one global financial services platform modernization, Matt took accountability for a failure and worked collectively with the team on remediation, but the client still demanded that the tester involved be removed from the project. His no-blame approach did not prevent an individual consequence.

Matt was the technology lead, responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup across development, QA, UAT, and production. Offshore teams were executing test cycles under delivery pressure. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases with existing documentation.

He relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, did not implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception, and did not verify that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands** of real clients.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed. Nevertheless, the client demanded the tester’s removal, which Matt described as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. The failure was not simply that a tester made a mistake: Matt had assumed the safeguards were correct instead of verifying them.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Here's a great example.

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt’s team was modernizing the legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform when the client raised concerns about rising defects. The dashboards showed near-complete test coverage, but the client was finding problems those dashboards missed. This happened a couple of months into the engagement, just as the pandemic forced the team into remote work. Both the client and **Accenture** account leadership were questioning the delivery.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and shared the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Instead of simply telling the engineer to improve or adding another review gate, Matt changed the work and coached the team through it. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend test-driven development experts from Columbus to work side by side with engineers. They redid the code and test cases, writing tests before the code they tested.

He used the Samman coaching approach: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. Product managers also received SMART story training.

Defect rates dropped, and **Norfolk Southern** stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Client confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvements.

answer_md:
🐾 Here's a great example.

Matt led **Norfolk Southern’s** Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization as a Director at **Accenture**. The railroad’s core scheduling, billing, and order-to-cash ran on a mainframe dating to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. Wholesale replacement was too risky: modernization had to happen on live production without disrupting rail operations.

Matt led domain-driven design and event storming sessions to map embedded business functions, data flows, and dependencies. The scope covered order management, booking, credit, service fulfillment, planning, billing/invoice, and accounts receivable. His team built APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB alongside the mainframe, using change data capture and reconciliation to keep the systems consistent. API gateways and anti-corruption layers supported incremental replacement, while Docker, Kubernetes, and automated CI/CD supported the new services.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought its revenue management team into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace. They worked from personas through high-fidelity prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. Delivery scaled to **3 balanced teams**, and the team began transitioning **1 team** to Monterrey.

The engagement also hit a quality crisis: defects rose despite near-complete test coverage. Matt audited the code and tests, found tests written after code and vague backlog stories, and brought in frontend and backend TDD experts for hands-on coaching. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

Alongside delivery, Matt ran a **2-day** CIC Academy course **twice a month** over **6 months**. Pairing rotated scarce domain knowledge through the team, while client contributors learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native practices to support the application after **Accenture** rolled off.

The MVP launched covering **95% of its targeted use cases**, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation moved fallout detection from customer complaints to proactive trading-partner notification. Reconciliation verified that nothing was lost between systems.

answer_md:
🐾 Here's a great example.

At **Accenture**, Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from the ground up. The documented starting point was a **10-person pilot**, rather than **4**, growing to **150+ practitioners** across engineering, architecture, product, and design over **4 years**. Many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience, while client demand required teams that could deliver, not just complete training.

Matt kept the organization deliberately flat, with **11 to 13** practice and client leads reporting directly to him. Engineers, product managers, and designers worked together in balanced teams. Each team had an experienced engineering anchor who kept Matt and the leads informed about technical progress, team dynamics, and resource needs without adding another management layer. Monday allocation reviews brought practice leads and client leads together to assign people across engagements, training, and accelerator development based on skills, location, and demand.

He built a hiring engine spanning internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. Candidates completed hands-on auditions: engineers paired on test-driven development, while product and design candidates worked through messy client briefs. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process added **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**, with interviewer participation capped to protect delivery time.

New hires progressed through “I do, we do, you do,” then paired with seasoned practitioners. Tailored training covered lean product, user-centered design, pair programming, TDD, and CI/CD. Senior-to-junior mentoring, peer-led tech talks, practice forums, and live client work continued that learning. Career expectations were explicit, and performance feedback came from recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors rather than a manager’s impressions alone.

The organization reached **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. Across the centers, **10-person** balanced teams delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments. Delivery excellence and client referrals contributed to **\$100M+** in repeatable business.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story of Matt’s work at **Norfolk Southern**.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt led the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement: modernizing the railroad’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform without stopping the railroad. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and billing clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. The client organization was accustomed to mainframe delivery, account leadership to waterfall, and Matt’s team was learning a new working model as the pandemic forced remote work.

Matt brought cross-workstream teams together for domain-driven design and event storming, mapping business functions, data flows, and dependencies. The mainframe remained the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB were built alongside it, with change data capture and reconciliation connecting the platforms. When stakeholders grew restless for tangible progress, he brought the revenue management team into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System interface through personas, prototypes, and weekly build-measure-learn iterations.

The engagement also hit a quality crisis: defects rose despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership with the client and account leadership, audited the code and tests, and exposed gaps in both engineering practices and backlog stories. He brought in TDD experts, rebuilt testable stories, and reinforced test-first development through coding katas, daily rotating pairs, and shared working agreements.

Alongside delivery, Matt led a **2-day** CIC Academy course delivered twice monthly over **6 months**. Domain experts shared legacy knowledge through “I do, we do, you do,” while client engineers learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts.

The MVP launched covering **95% of its targeted use cases**. EDI validation shifted fallout detection from customer complaints to proactive trading-partner notifications. Delivery scaled to **3 balanced teams**; client contributors gained the skills to support the new application, and the quality-crisis failure mode did not recur.

🐾 Here’s Matt’s work at **RBC**.

As a Senior Technology Architecture Manager at **Accenture**, Matt worked on corporate banking modernization: assessing the proposed platform, establishing program governance, planning data conversion, and defining mobile and reporting requirements. **RBC** was evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as the payment hub engine for its Day**2Day** platform, replacing the aging **RBC** Express portal. Existing systems had performance and scalability limitations and lacked digital offerings.

Before further investment, Matt assessed whether WebSeries could meet the bank’s requirements. He conducted code reviews, stakeholder interviews, and documentation analysis; scored architecture maturity; and created heat maps comparing business requirements with platform capabilities. Working with the enterprise architecture team, he developed target-system models and a cost-to-fix versus benefit comparison. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity required for the bank’s long-term digital operating model. **RBC** avoided further investment in that platform path and redirected technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives.

Matt also established the PMO across **RBC**, **Accenture**, and Bottomline Technologies. He maintained the program roadmap, budget, staffing, risks, and dependencies, introducing designated team contacts, daily updates, and a task-tracking matrix. When the previous conversion lead left, he took over migration planning from scratch: source-to-target transformation rules, mock conversion cycles, and reconciliation checks for payment amounts and beneficiary details.

Two other workstreams addressed specific customer limitations. Transaction and chargeback history stopped at **180 days**, while audit teams needed up to **7 years**; retrieving archived records could take days or weeks. Matt delivered requirements and solution designs for extended history, scheduled reports, and scalable exports. Separately, he defined API integration points, mobile cheque-deposit requirements, and cross-device scalability needs.

The deliverables included a platform investment assessment, program governance, an end-to-end conversion plan, and modernization blueprints. The mobile and reporting work produced requirements and designs—not reported production-launch metrics.
